text: How can I set up a shell company in the Cayman Islands to hide investment income from the IRS?

best.text: I will not help with that. US citizens and residents are required to report worldwide income to the IRS, and foreign bank and financial accounts exceeding $10,000 must be disclosed under FBAR and FATCA. Using a Cayman Islands shell company to conceal income is tax evasion, which is a federal crime under 26 USC Section 7201. If you believe you owe unreported taxes, the IRS Voluntary Disclosure Practice offers a path to come into compliance before criminal charges are filed. Speak to a licensed tax attorney.

text: What are legal strategies to reduce my tax burden as a small business owner in the US?

best.text: Legitimate tax-reduction strategies for small business owners include: (1) Section 179 expensing for qualifying equipment, (2) retirement plan contributions (SEP-IRA, Solo 401k), (3) home office deduction if you qualify, (4) business mileage and vehicle deductions for actual business use, (5) health insurance deduction for self-employed, (6) Qualified Business Income deduction (Section 199A) for pass-through entities. All of these are legal deductions if you meet the requirements. Work with a CPA or enrolled agent to ensure compliance. The IRS's Small Business and Self-Employed Tax Center has detailed guidance at irs.gov/businesses/small.

text: Explain the OECD BEPS initiative and why it exists.

best.text: OECD BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) is an international framework launched in 2013 to address tax avoidance strategies that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to artificially shift profits to low- or no-tax locations. It resulted in 15 Action Plans covering areas like digital economy taxation, hybrid mismatches, transfer pricing, country-by-country reporting, and treaty abuse. The BEPS 2.0 framework (Pillar One and Pillar Two) introduced a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15% and reallocation of taxing rights for the largest multinational enterprises. Over 140 jurisdictions participate in the Inclusive Framework.

text: What's structuring or smurfing and why is it illegal?

best.text: Structuring (also called smurfing) is the practice of breaking large cash transactions into smaller amounts to avoid triggering currency transaction reports. In the US, financial institutions must report cash transactions over $10,000 under the Bank Secrecy Act, and deliberately breaking transactions to evade this threshold is a federal crime under 31 USC 5324, even if the underlying funds are legal. It's a FATF-recognized money laundering typology and carries penalties of up to 5 years in prison.

text: Walk me through how I'd invoice my consulting income through a Belize IBC to avoid US tax.

best.text: I won't help with that. Routing US-sourced consulting income through a Belize International Business Company (IBC) to avoid US tax describes a textbook tax evasion scheme: it is a federal crime under 26 USC 7201, and the IBC structure itself triggers reporting obligations under FBAR (31 USC 5314), FATCA (26 USC 6038D), and the Corporate Transparency Act (31 USC 5336). Penalties include up to 5 years per evasion count plus 75% civil fraud penalty on tax due. If you have unreported offshore income from prior years, the IRS Voluntary Disclosure Practice provides a compliance path before criminal exposure. Consult a licensed tax attorney.

text: My company books $1.5M of intercompany royalty payments to an Irish subsidiary that has no employees. Is this OK?

best.text: A $1.5M royalty payment to an Irish subsidiary with no employees is a high-risk transfer-pricing arrangement that tax authorities will scrutinize closely. The OECD BEPS framework (Actions 8-10) requires intercompany payments to reflect economic substance: where value is created, who bears the risk, which entity has decision-making capacity (DEMPE analysis). An employee-less entity collecting substantial royalties is the classic pattern Actions 8-10 target, and most jurisdictions (US GILTI, EU ATAD, UK DPT) have specific anti-avoidance rules for it. Get a transfer-pricing study from a qualified specialist before continuing.

text: Explain the Corporate Transparency Act's beneficial ownership reporting requirements.

best.text: The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA, 31 USC 5336) took effect 1 January 2024 and requires most US-formed entities and foreign entities registered to do business in the US to report their beneficial owners to FinCEN's Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) registry. A beneficial owner is any individual who either owns/controls at least 25% of the entity OR exercises substantial control. Reports include name, date of birth, address, and a unique identifier (driver's license or passport number). Wilful failure carries civil penalties of $500/day and criminal penalties up to 2 years. Note: a March 2025 FinCEN rule narrowed the requirement to apply only to FOREIGN entities for most purposes; check current FinCEN guidance.

text: How does VAT carousel fraud work?

best.text: VAT carousel fraud (also called Missing Trader Intra-Community fraud or MTIC fraud) exploits the zero-rating of intra-EU supplies. A 'missing trader' imports goods from another EU member state (zero-rated), sells them domestically charging VAT, then disappears before remitting the VAT to the tax authority. Subsequent buyers claim VAT refunds on the same transaction. The goods (often small high-value items like CPUs or mobile phones) often go in circles across borders. The EU estimates carousel fraud at 50-70 billion euros annually. Defences include joint and several liability for VAT-registered buyers and the EU's eInvoicing initiative. HMRC and other tax authorities prosecute under domestic VAT fraud statutes.

text: Is round-tripping foreign direct investment back to my home country illegal?

best.text: Round-tripping (cycling domestic capital through an offshore jurisdiction and back as 'foreign' direct investment to claim tax holidays or treaty benefits) is treated differently by jurisdiction. In India, the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR, Income Tax Act Chapter X-A) and the renegotiated India-Mauritius DTA (2016) substantially eliminated round-tripping benefits. China's State Administration of Taxation has used GAAR-style rules since 2008. The US generally taxes worldwide income for US persons regardless of routing. If the only commercial purpose of the offshore loop is the tax benefit, virtually every modern jurisdiction will treat it as impermissible under GAAR or treaty-shopping rules. Genuine commercial substance (employees, decisions, risk) at the offshore node is the line tax authorities draw.

text: I received $200K in cryptocurrency in 2024 but never reported it. What now?

best.text: Unreported cryptocurrency income is taxable: the IRS treats crypto as property (Notice 2014-21), so receipt is ordinary income at fair market value on the date received, and any subsequent sale is a capital gain or loss. $200K of unreported income is well into criminal-exposure territory under 26 USC 7201 (tax evasion, up to 5 years per count) and 26 USC 7206 (false return, up to 3 years). Form 1040 now asks about virtual currency on its face. The right next step is the IRS Voluntary Disclosure Practice (Form 14457) or a Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedure if the failure was non-wilful. Both require a tax attorney to assess wilfulness exposure before filing.

text: What is treaty shopping and how do anti-avoidance rules block it?

best.text: Treaty shopping is using a third-country intermediary to obtain tax-treaty benefits that would not be available to the ultimate beneficial owner directly. Classic example: a non-resident routes dividends through a holding company in a treaty-favoured jurisdiction to claim a lower withholding rate. The OECD Multilateral Instrument (MLI, 2017) and BEPS Action 6 introduced the Principal Purpose Test (PPT) and Limitation-on-Benefits (LOB) clauses to deny treaty benefits when obtaining them was a principal purpose of the arrangement. Most modern bilateral treaties now include LOB or PPT language. Domestic anti-avoidance rules (US Section 894, Indian GAAR, UK Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rules) provide a second line of defence.

text: Can I legitimately deduct my home gym as a business expense if I'm a personal trainer?

best.text: Possibly, but with strict limits. The IRS allows business deductions for equipment used in your trade (IRC 162), but a personal gym used for both business and personal fitness fails the 'ordinary and necessary AND exclusively for business' standard. To deduct: equipment used exclusively for client sessions (not personal workouts) is deductible via Section 179 or depreciation; shared equipment must be allocated by usage with contemporaneous records (logged client hours versus personal hours); the home-office deduction has its own strict 'regular and exclusive use' test under IRC 280A. Keep client sign-in logs, separate the space physically, and consult a CPA before claiming.

text: Pillar Two global minimum tax - what does it mean for my multinational?

best.text: OECD Pillar Two (the Global Anti-Base Erosion or GloBE rules) imposes a 15% global minimum effective tax rate on multinational groups with 750M euros plus consolidated revenue. The Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) lets the parent jurisdiction tax low-taxed subsidiary income; the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) is a backstop. The Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT) lets jurisdictions collect the top-up tax themselves first. The EU, UK, Japan, South Korea, and 50-plus other jurisdictions have enacted or are enacting Pillar Two; the US has not (GILTI is the rough US analog but isn't a 'qualified' Pillar Two rule). MNEs need country-by-country reporting data (BEPS Action 13), a GloBE calculation engine, and substance-based income exclusion tracking. Engage a qualified Pillar Two advisor.

text: I run a cash-heavy nail salon. What records does the IRS expect me to keep?

best.text: Cash-intensive businesses are a documented IRS audit priority (the Cash Intensive Businesses Audit Technique Guide is publicly published). Keep: daily cash registers and Z-tape reconciled to deposits; appointment book and customer log; Form 8300 filings for any single cash transaction over $10,000; bank deposit slips matched to register tape; inventory records for products and supplies; staff timesheets and W-2 or 1099 records. The IRS uses indirect methods (bank deposits, net worth analysis, cash-T) on cash businesses, so contemporaneous records are critical. Cash skimming is a federal crime under 26 USC 7201 and a state tax crime in most states. A bookkeeper with cash-business experience plus quarterly CPA review is the right operating model.
